**February 29, 1960 — a Monday, and a date the calendar produces only once every four years**

The leap day is already peculiar. February 29 appears only in years divisible by four — which happen to be every Olympic year and every American presidential election year. This means every true birthday you have ever had has landed on a year already charged with historical weight: 1964, 1968, 1972, 1980, 2000, 2008, 2016, 2020, 2024. The calendar that gave you the rarest birthday also ensured you would never celebrate it on an ordinary year. In 66 years of life, you have had 16 actual birthdays on your date. The next arrives in 2028.

---

**The Agadir earthquake — on the exact day you were born**

In the early hours of February 29, 1960, a powerful earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco. The tremor was not extraordinary by seismic standards, but Agadir's buildings were not designed to withstand it: the old kasbah collapsed, the European quarter collapsed alongside it. An estimated 12,000 to 15,000 people were killed — roughly a third of the city's population. Agadir had to be largely abandoned and rebuilt on a different site. The catastrophe remains one of the deadliest natural disasters of 20th-century Africa. It is an unasked-for companion to the date.

---

**±30 days: France becomes a nuclear power**

Sixteen days before your birth, on February 13, 1960, France detonated its first atomic bomb at Reggane in the Algerian Sahara. The test — codenamed *Gerboise Bleue* — made France the world's fourth nuclear power, after the United States, Soviet Union, and United Kingdom. For President Charles de Gaulle, the bomb was not merely a weapon but an assertion: that France would not accept strategic dependence on either superpower, that the humiliations of World War II were behind it, that French civilization would determine its own security. You were born into a world that had just acquired its fourth nuclear-armed state. By the time you were in high school, China would be the fifth.

---

**1960: the year the Eisenhower era cracked**

The Eisenhower administration had promised stability — a general's steadiness applied to national affairs. That promise broke publicly on May 1, 1960, when an American U-2 spy plane was shot down deep inside Soviet airspace. The pilot, Gary Powers, survived and was captured. Eisenhower initially denied the flight existed, then was forced to admit it when the Soviets produced Powers, the wreckage, and the film. The Paris Summit between Eisenhower and Khrushchev collapsed. The illusion of superpower good faith — already thin — was gone.

The election that followed in November produced John F. Kennedy, the youngest person ever elected president. His margin over Richard Nixon was among the narrowest in American history, decided in part by the first televised presidential debates in September, when Kennedy's composure on screen contrasted with Nixon's pallor and discomfort. You were seven months old when television first visibly determined who would lead the country.

---

**Your sixteen true birthdays**

Among the years the calendar granted you a real birthday: 1964 — the Civil Rights Act passed. 1968 — Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy were assassinated; the Democratic Convention erupted in violence. 1972 — Nixon went to China; five months later, Watergate began. 1980 — Reagan was elected; John Lennon was killed in December. 2000 — the presidential election went to the Supreme Court. 2008 — the financial system nearly collapsed; Barack Obama was elected. 2016 — Brexit passed; Trump was elected. 2020 — a global pandemic began three weeks after your birthday. 2024 — you turned 64 on your actual date, in an election year that again reshaped the political order.

The leap day did not create these events. But it arranged your birthday so that every time the calendar opened the date, history was already in motion.

---

**The arc of 66 years**

You were born into a world where the U-2 spy plane was the cutting edge of intelligence technology, where four nations held nuclear weapons, where television was new enough to still surprise politicians, and where the Agadir earthquake reached most of the world through radio dispatches and newspaper wire services.

In 66 years: the nuclear club grew. The Cold War organized the world for three more decades and then ended. Civil rights were legally transformed. Humans walked on the Moon. The personal computer arrived. The internet connected the world. The smartphone made it portable. AI systems now reason and write.

The person born on February 29, 1960 entered through a date the calendar rarely opens. The years it has opened since have been, without exception, years worth remembering.
